PHYS 105.d: Rigorous, mathematical foundation in classical mechanics. Topics include Newtonian mechanics; motion of particles in one, two and three dimensions; central force motion; moving coordinate systems; mechanics of continuous media; oscillations; normal modes; Lagrange's equations; and Hamiltonian methods.

PHYS 109.d: Introduces the physics of soft materials. In this course we will use a physics based approach to study the structure and assembly of a variety materials including liquid crystals, polymers, colloidal systems and surfactants including biological examples.

PHYS 115.t: Electrodynamics Core II Waves and Dynamic Electromagnetic Fields
PHYS 115.d: Waves and advanced electromagnetic fields, including radiation and special relativity. General discussion of waves and vibrations. Review of Maxwell's equations and discussion on conserved quantities in electromagnetic fields. Electromagnetic waves, potential formulations, radiation from moving charges, and special relativity.

o.x: Self AP Physics C Elect & Mag

PHYS 126.d: Introduces the exciting and thought-provoking physics of special relativity through a half-semester minicourse. Topics include hallmark experiments; Lorentz transformations; time dilation and length contraction; relativistic optics; tensor techniques; mass, energy, and momentum; relativistic mechanics; and relativistic electricity and magnetism.

PHYS 127.t: Machine Learning and Statistics for Physics and Astronomy

PHYS 128.d: Introduces general relativity. Includes an overview of special relativity, an introduction to differential geometry, and application of general relativity to study topics including black holes, gravitational lensing, and the expanding Universe.

PHYS 138.d: Applies quantum mechanics to solve problems in atomic physics. Includes two parts: (1) the study of perturbative techniques, variational principle and adiabatic approximation, all of which widely used in modern physics; (2) the study of the quantum theory of angular momentum.

PHYS 144.t: Modern Atomic, Molecular, and Optical Physics

PHYS 160.d: Provides a rigorous foundation in physics laboratory techniques, with an emphasis on hands-on laboratory training. The nature of the experiments available to students cover a range of modern topics, from nonlinear dynamics and chaos through nonlinear optics and spectroscopy. Emphasis is placed on error estimation, data analysis, and interpretation.

PHYS 173.t: Teaching for Learning: Instructional Learning Assistant Pedagogy Course
PHYS 173.d: Offers pedagogical training for students during their first semester serving in the Learning Assistant Program and focuses on integrating education theory, pedagogy, and practice. Addresses practical concerns and introduces relevant topics from education literature to support students' experience as Learning Assistants. Required for students in their first semester in the Learning Assistant Program. Open only to students hired as Instructional Learning Assistants during the same semester.

PHYS 174.d: In the fast-growing research area of quantum computing and quantum information, the goal of this course is not only to guide students in learning basic concepts, but also to introduce students with recent progresses in this area. Course materials span from fundamental concepts of quantum computing, quantum algorithm, physical implementation, to recent progresses on quantum advantage and special purpose quantum computers. The materials will be organized into three themes: (1) basics concepts, (2) the implementation of quantum computing, and (3) recent progress in noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.

o.x: Self AP Physics C Elect & Mag

PHYS 180.d: Most processes encountered in nature are inherently nonlinear. This course introduces the main topics of low-dimensional nonlinear systems, with applications to a wide variety of disciplines, including physics, engineering, mathematics, chemistry, and biology. Specific topics include maps and flows in one and two dimensions, phase portraits, bifurcations, chaos, and fractals.

PHYS 196.d: Gives upper-division undergraduate Physics majors further opportunity to engage in laboratory, field, theoretical, and/or computational research under the supervision of a faculty member on a topic of mutual interest. The seminar portion of this course supports students in writing and orally presenting their senior thesis.

PHYS 201.t: Teaching and Learning in the Sciences

PHYS 209.d: Introduces the physics of soft materials. Uses a physics based approach to study the structure and assembly of a variety of materials including liquid crystals, polymers, colloidal systems and surfactants including biological examples.

PHYS 212.d: Topics include: General principles of statistical mechanics including microcanonical, macrocanonical and grand canonical ensembles, fluctuations and equilibrium. Thermodynamics including Legendre transforms and Maxwell relations, fluctuations and stability and Landau theory. Quantum statistical mechanics including Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac statistics. Undergraduate-level knowledge of thermal physics and statistical mechanics equivalent to PHYS 108 is required.

PHYS 227.t: Machine Learning and Statistics for Physics and Astronomy

PHYS 230.t: Computation and Modeling for Interdisciplinary Biophysical Sciences, Biomaterials and Biotechnology

PHYS 231.t: Imaging and Spectroscopy for Interdisciplinary Biophysical Sciences, Biomaterials and Biotechnology

PHYS 234.t: Frontiers of Molecular and Cellular Biotechnology
PHYS 234.d: Current state-of-the-art techniques and concepts in molecular and cellular biotechnology will be introduced. Topics include bioinformatics, molecular dynamics simulations, systems modeling, protein engineering, biomolecular assemblies, drug and gene delivery, recombinant DNA, tissue engineering, single molecule measurements, optogenetics, CRISPR, in vivo imaging, biomaterials, bioelectronics.

PHYS 237.d: Introductory Quantum Mechanics starting with simple Quantum two-state systems and one-dimensional problems, Uncertainty relations, Solution of Schrodinger's equation for important two and three dimensional physical situations, Angular momentum, identical particles and spin statistics. Hydrogen and multi-electron atoms. Undergraduate-level knowledge of quantum mechanics equivalent to PHYS 137 is required.

PHYS 244.t: Modern Atomic, Molecular, and Optical Physics

PHYS 274.d: Teaches a broad range of topics in the fast-growing area of quantum computing. Course materials span from fundamental concepts of quantum computing and quantum algorithms to recent progress in quantum advantage and special-purpose quantum computers. This course is suitable for graduate students who want to learn about quantum computing, who are preparing to do research on quantum information, or who are currently conducting research on quantum technology.

PHYS 280.d: Most processes encountered in nature are inherently nonlinear. This course introduces the main topics of low-dimensional nonlinear systems, with applications to a wide variety of disciplines, including physics, engineering, mathematics, chemistry, and biology. Specific topics include maps and flows in one and two dimensions, phase portraits, bifurcations, chaos, and fractals.

PHYS 293.d: Introduces graduate and undergraduate students to cutting-edge research in physics conducted on-site and elsewhere, and gives them an opportunity to meet researchers and faculty from other universities/research institutions. This is a colloquium series with talks on a wide range of research topics in physics. Speakers for the colloquia are primarily invited researchers from other institutions. Some of the seminars additionally showcase the research performed by UC Merced Physics faculty, postdoctoral researchers and graduate students.

POLI 001.d: A general introduction to political institutions and political behavior in the United States. Specific topics include the U.S. Constitution, Congress, the presidency, the federal judiciary, political parties, interest groups, mass public opinion, elections, and voting behavior.

POLI 003.d: Introduction to the cross-national study of political institutions and behavior. Formal and informal aspects of politics in selected countries are covered, as are comparative research methods.

POLI 005.d: Introduction to the study of the politics of conflict and war, diplomacy, international cooperation, and international institutions.

POLI 009.d: Examination of political and social mobilization at the local level, including strategies for organization and advocacy.

POLI 010.d: Overview of the application of social scientific methods to the study of politics. Covers research design, hypothesis testing, measurement, and a variety of methodological approaches (e.g. experiments, descriptive and inferential statistics, qualitative analysis) to answering political questions.

POLI 101.d: Powers, constraints, and behavior of the U.S. president and executive branch. Includes specific topics such as legislative-executive interactions, presidential control of the bureaucracy, nomination campaigns and general elections, and public opinion and the presidency.

POLI 102.d: Structure, function, and politics of the U.S. court system, with a particular focus on the selection of judges, judicial decision making, external political influences on the judiciary, and the impact of court decisions.

POLI 112.t: Public Policy: Analysis, Strategy, and Impact
POLI 112.d: Introduces public policy and policy analysis. The material builds practical skills for effecting change while developing a theoretical understanding of policymakers’ goals – and how these goals are pursued. Emphasizes methods and strategies applicable across policy spheres. Students will strengthen their proficiency in asking relevant questions, assessing problems from multiple perspectives, and using a variety of analytical tools (rooted in political science, economics, psychology, and more) to evaluate and solve policy problems.

POLI 138.d: Examines why some countries are poor while others are prosperous, highlighting the role of political factors and political institutions.

POLI 150.d: Investigation of the causes of international conflict and war, the conduct of war, its ultimate termination, and the possibility of its prevention.

POLI 157.t: Civil War, Insurgency, and Other Forms of Sub-State Conflict and Social Unrest

POLI 160.d: The formation of U.S. foreign policy, with an emphasis on the modern era and an introduction to analytical tools for understanding current foreign policy issues and debates.

POLI 171.d: Considers whether politics as portrayed on film differs from political reality as understood through political science, and further uses films as vehicles for better understanding an array of topics from political science, including legislative behavior, elections, presidential politics, local politics, war, and international relations.

POLI 172.d: Teaches students the basics of game-theoretic modeling, and how those models have been used to explain human behavior across a number of social and political settings.

POLI 174.d: Trains students to think critically about data, the patterns they reveal, and when such patterns are most likely to depict causal effects. Explores relationships between variables and how/why data can be misunderstood. As an applied course, offers students the opportunity to develop a working knowledge of programming in R that will lend itself to a variety of quantitative/computational tasks. Focuses on select forms of data processing and analysis relevant to studying government, politics, and policy.

POLI 190.d: Topics in Political Science selected by instructor.

POLI 194H.d: Guides students through the writing of the thesis. Students will present completed theses and evaluate portions of each other’s projects.

POLI 210.t: Quantitative Analysis of Political Data, I

POLI 211.t: Quantitative Analysis of Political Data, II
POLI 211.d: Provides an in-depth introduction to ordinary least squares regression analysis and its use in political science.

POLI 212.t: Quantitative Analysis of Political Data, III

POLI 214.d: Provides a survey of more advanced empirical tools, with a particular focus on causal inference. Covers a variety of research designs and statistical methods for causal inference, including experiments, matching, regression, panel methods, difference-in-differences, instrumental variable estimation, and regression discontinuity designs. Applications are drawn from various fields including political science, public policy, economics, social psychology, and sociology.

POLI 219.t: Special Topics in Political Science Methodology

POLI 230.t: Institutions and Institutional Change in Comparative Perspectives

POLI 249.t: Special Topics in Political Institutions and Political Economy
POLI 249.d: A special, instructor-selected topic in political institutions and/or political economy.

POLI 252.d: An in-depth examination of American public opinion. We will cover concepts and tools, including technical issues of sampling and measurement, as well as the origins and structure of political attitudes and specific areas of public opinion research such as approval of political institutions, war attitudes, and tolerance.

POLI 269.t: Special Topics in Political Cognition and Behavior

POLI 293.t: Critical Assessment of Political Science Research

PSY 001.d: Introduction to psychology as a science of behavior, including history, research methods, biological bases of behavior, cognition, personality, social behavior, psychological disorders, techniques of therapy and applied science.

PSY 010.d: Design and analysis of psychological research including experimental design, correlational research, and descriptive and inferential statistics. Students in the Psychology major or minor must take this course before taking any upper division Psychology courses.

PSY 015.d: Develops an understanding of broad perspectives and common theories within the field of Research Methods in Psychology and applies this knowledge to better understand the world we live in (locally and globally). Demonstrates ability to interpret current events and other real-world scenarios within the framework of perspectives and theories related to research methods in psychology. Some research related issues include ethics, sampling, study design, reliability and validity, data analysis, and the reporting of results.

PSY 107.t: Analysis of Variance in Psychological Research

PSY 111.d: Surveys the application of psychology to the criminal justice system, including public policy, sanity, competency, eyewitness testimony and treatment of mentally ill offenders. Introduces to topics surrounding forensic psychology, as well as extensions to this field.

PSY 120.d: Introduces students to a breadth of topics in health psychology, behavioral medicine, and public health. Particular emphasis is placed on the roles of psychological processes in altering physical and mental health, promoting well-being, preventing illness, and treating disease.

PSY 124.d: Focuses on the differential effects of environmental factors and behavior on human health. In examining the determinants of health, discusses issues related to ethnic, cultural, and gender psychology, risk behavior, behavioral medicine, psychosocial epidemiology, and policy.

PSY 129A.d: Introduces and studies a special topic or problem of psychological interest in the domain of physical health and well-being. Each class will have a specific focus which will be defined by the instructor of the course on a semester-by-semester basis. Example topics include identity and health, motivation and well-being, stress, coping, and emotion, and patient-physician communication. Course content will include both historical perspectives on the topic as well as recent, empirically informed theories and findings.

PSY 130.d: Critical review of the research and theories on the development of infants and children. Covers cognitive, biological, social, personality, and emotional development, among others. Emphasis on integrating across areas of development, as well as the relative contributions of biology and experience.

PSY 132.d: Covers theoretical and empirical research related to the study of child and adolescent development in the family context. The major theories of family research will be covered, including ecological theory, family systems theories, attachment theory, and sociocultural theories. Through the lens of these perspectives, we will examine recent research on various relevant topics, including connections between family and school, parenting practices, sibling relationships, and the broader cultural context in which families live.

PSY 133.t: Neurodevelopmental Cognitive, Language and Learning Disorders

PSY 139A.d: Introduces and studies a special topic or problem of psychological interest in the domain of development. Each class will have a specific focus which will be defined by the instructor of the course on a semester-by-semester basis. Example topics include identity development, child and family well-being, family communication, culture and development, aging, and lifespan emotional development. Course content will include both historical perspectives on the topic as well as recent, empirically informed theories and findings.

PSY 140.d: Major theoretical approaches to clinical psychology, including psychoanalysis, existentialism, humanism, systems theory, and behavioral approaches. A review of what clinical psychologists do, including assessment methods, professional roles, and approaches to treatment.

PSY 142.d: Descriptive and functional account of behavioral disorders, with primary consideration given to neurotic and psychotic behavior.

PSY 143.d: Review of scientific knowledge and approaches to learning about major psychological disorders in childhood, including adolescence. Examples are anxiety, attention deficit, autistic, and substance use disorders. Interventions implemented to prevent or treat these disorders are also examined.

PSY 149A.t: Topics in Clinical and Counseling Psychology

PSY 149B.t: Advanced Topics in Clinical and Counseling Psychology

PSY 150.d: Examines how individuals are unique and similar to other people. Covers major theories in personality that attempt to describe human nature and empirical research on individual differences and personality development.

PSY 151.t: The Psychology of Stereotyping and Prejudice

PSY 152.t: Psychological Perspectives on Cultural, Racial and Ethnic Diversity
PSY 152.d: Issues that bear upon race, ethnicity, and culture, such as the cultural specificity of psychological theories, cultural influences on child development, ethnic identity, psychological issues in immigration, ethnic and racial prejudice, and assessment and interventions with culturally diverse and ethnic minority populations.

PSY 153.d: Examines how psychologists have addressed questions relating to gender in past and present-day research. The goal is to understand what "gender" is, and how and when gender matters in our evaluations of ourselves and in our interactions with others. It will have four themes: (1) defining gender and sex and challenging the binary system; (2) stereotypes and sexism, (3) gender in relationships; and (4) gender and well-being. It encourages students to think critically about the material, engage with the assignments, and to ask questions during office hours, on the discussion board, or through email. Students will be challenged to think about how their personal experiences can be better understood based on theory and research around the psychology of gender.

PSY 155.d: Provides an overview of the field of emotion. A general theoretical overview will be complemented by examining specific topics of emotion, highlighting the interdisciplinary nature of emotion research across multiple fields of study, including psychology, sociology, linguistics, and anthropology.

PSY 156.d: Behavior of the individual in social situations, surveying problems of social cognition, social interaction, group tensions, norm development, attitudes, values, public opinion, status.

PSY 157.d: Surveys the psychological science of close relationships, including interpersonal attraction, communication, interdependence, friendship, love, sex, conflict, violence, breakups and relationship loss.

PSY 159A.t: Topics in Social and Personality Psychology
PSY 159A.d: Introduces and studies a special topic or problem of psychological interest in the domain of social and personality psychology. Each class will have a specific focus which will be defined by the instructor of the course on a semester-by-semester basis. Example topics include personality assessment, personal and social identity, attitudes, persuasion, social intervention, and individual differences. Course content will include both historical perspectives on the topic as well as recent, empirically informed theories and findings.

PSY 159B.t: Advanced Topics in Social and Personality Psychology

PSY 160.d: Introduction to human information processing, mental representation and transformation, imagery, attention, memory, language processing, concept formation, problem solving, and computer simulation.

PSY 170.d: How psychology is applied to industrial and organizational problems, including workplace testing, personnel issues, advertising, etc.

PSY 175.d: Surveys existing knowledge of human sexual behavior; physiological, anatomical, psychological, and cultural components; normative sexual functioning. Includes topics as sexual deviation, sexual dysfunctions, and types of treatment are also considered.

PSY 180.d: Explores the relationship of brain structure and function to behavior, motivation, emotion, language, and learning in humans and other animals. Reviews research methods used in physiological psychology and neuroscience.

PSY 186.d: Provides a general background concerning therapeutic drugs and the psychological impact of these drugs. Covers the neuro and pharmacodynamic process of drugs most commonly prescribed for psychiatric conditions and diagnoses. Applies to students coming from a broad range of backgrounds, including psychology, biology, or chemistry. However, background knowledge in these topics areas is not required—the material is presented at an introductory but comprehensive level.

PSY 191.d: Provides an in-depth treatment of various facets to the Psychology major. It is intended to satisfy the Psychology major’s Culminating Experience for the degree. Covers problems and research-based inquires in a variety of sub-fields within Psychology, including: health, developmental, quantitative, social, clinical, and more. Also covers important elements such as APA writing style, how to present results, and ethics in psychological research.

PSY 191L.t: Laboratory for Culminating Experience in Psychology
PSY 191L.d: Provides students with hands-on training in producing a product for scientific communication as it is a laboratory course attached to the culminating experience in psychology (PSY 191). Specifically, students will receive specific training in psychological scientific writing and presentation and will have the opportunity to receive feedback specific to the individual projects that they will present in PSY191.

PSY 194H.d: The Honors in Psychological Sciences course is intended for advanced-level students seeking to complete an independent research project in collaboration with a faculty advisor in Psychological Sciences. This course is intended to provide structure and guidance for conducting an independent research project, concrete deadlines and feedback during the research process, and a forum within which to share and present research findings with fellow honors students in Psychological Science.

PSY 200A.t: Professional Seminar for First-Year Graduate Students I

PSY 200B.t: Professional Seminar for First-Year Graduate Students II
PSY 200B.d: A two semester sequence required of and limited to first-year Ph.D. students in Psychology. Survey of major issues in contemporary psychology with their historical backgrounds.

PSY 202B.d: Topics covered include: regression; multiple regression; path analysis; introduction to structural equation modeling with latent variables; introduction to multilevel modeling.

PSY 209.t: Longitudinal Data Analysis and Bayesian Extensions

PSY 215.t: Essential Mathematics for Quantitative Social Research

PSY 221.d: A survey of selected topics in health psychology not covered in PSY 220. This may include psychological perspectives on major chronic disease, quality of life in people with health conditions, pediatric psychology, aging and health, and the interface between public health and health psychology.

PSY 239.d: Surveys current topics and research methods in developmental psychology, including language acquisition, social cognition, emotion understanding, adolescent development, family systems, and cultural processes in development. Topics will be selected based on student interests. Students will be responsible for presenting original research ideas based on supplied readings and guest speakers will be incorporated.

PSY 251.t: The Psychology of Prejudice and Stereotyping

PSY 263.t: Language and Communication in Everyday Life

PSY 290.d: Under faculty supervision, group of students meets each week for a semester in a student-led study group to pursue a specific topic of their choice that is not covered in other department courses.

PSY 299.t: Directed Individual Research and Study in Psychology

PH 001.d: An introduction to Public Health, including i) scientific tools, ii) biomedical basis, iii) societal determinants of health, iv) environmental health, iv) role of the medical care system, v) population level interventions, vi) health communication and promotion, and vii) challenges facing public health.

PH 005.d: Overviews the dynamic factors that produce global health challenges, including demographic changes, conflict, human rights abuses, migration, travel, food production and distribution, water resources, and market forces and economic factors. Examines their responsibilities towards global health as global citizens.

PH 010.d: Introduces methods and concepts of statistics and applies these principles to public health, medicine, and the health sciences. Topics include descriptive statistics, data visualization, probability, distributions, estimation, hypothesis testing, and confidence levels.

PH 100.d: Introduces students to the basic concepts of epidemiology, and to selected specific areas of interest of this quantitative discipline. Topics include disease surveillance and measurement, risk factor evaluation (e.g., study designs), analyses of epidemiologic data, and critical analyses of threats to validity.

PH 102.d: Health promotion is the process of enabling people to increase control over, and to improve, their health. This course provides students with an overview of the principles of health promotion and various theories developed to change health behavior and promote the health of individuals and societies.

PH 103.d: Explores the science and practice of health communication. Describes the essentials for effective health communication and social marketing, reaching target audiences, developing and testing effective messages, and evaluating the impact of a communication campaign.

PH 105.t: Introduction to US Health Care System

PH 106.d: Provides students with an overview of health policy and related policymaking processes in the U.S. Covers a range of local, state, and federal policies to improve population health outcomes, including health care policies (e.g., Medicare, Medicaid) and public health policies to promote health, prevent disease, and address health disparities.

PH 111.d: Social epidemiology is the branch of epidemiology that explores how social forces affect human health and well being. In particular it asks how social interactions, human activities, social conditions, social problems, and other social arrangements affect determinants of health and yield differential health outcomes.

PH 112.t: Research Methods: Health Services Research and Public Health
PH 112.d: Introduces research in the public health, health services research, and healthcare evaluation. Includes both qualitative and quantitative research methods, using examples of research across a range of areas in health.

PH 113.d: Examines predictors of health for refugees and immigrant to the US, and their descendants, paying particular attention to Latinos. Examines the effects of acculturation on health, and shifts in health and health-related behavioral outcomes between refugees or immigrants and second and third (and beyond) generations. Students who have not completed PH 102 can enroll in CCST 113/PH 113 with permission of the instructor.

PH 115.t: Geographic Information Systems Mapping for Public Health

PH 117.t: Decolonizing Methodologies in Public Health Research

PH 118.d: Introduces public health nutrition and the roles of public health professionals. There will be an emphasis on definition, identification, and prevention of nutrition related disease. Nutrition assessment tools, the current state of evidence, diet and disease, and public health nutrition strategies and approaches will be examined. Students will learn basic public health nutrition concepts and apply them to their own lives and real-world issues through a variety of assignments and activities.

PH 119.d: Provides an introduction to mental illness in the United States from the perspective of public health. Explores current research and debates surrounding the definition, epidemiology, prevention, and treatment of mental disorders, focusing on a public health approach. Critically discusses the history of beliefs about mentally ill individuals and how these beliefs have influenced mental health policy, systems, services and treatment over the last century.

PH 120.t: Unintentional and Intentional Injury: Description, Prevention, and Research

PH 123.d: Examines substance use and disorders through a public health lens. Explores what drugs are, why people use them, when use becomes harmful, and the costs of prohibition. Investigates harm reduction strategies, models of control, and the health, social, and policy impacts of specific substances.

PH 124.d: Focuses on the differential effects of environmental factors and behavior on human health. In examining the determinants of health, discusses issues related to ethnic, cultural, and gender psychology, risk behavior, behavioral medicine, psychosocial epidemiology, and policy.

PH 130.t: Does the Dose Make the Poison? Introduction to Toxicology and Risk Assessment
PH 130.d: Explores how toxicology is used to understand how humans respond to chemicals in the environment and how the information is used to compute health-based exposure benchmarks. Toxicology is a multidisciplinary experimental science that combines chemistry, biology, and physiology to determine whether substances we are exposed to in the environment are likely to harm our health.

PH 180H.t: Unmasking the Past: Epidemics and Public Health in the U.S.

PH 181.d: Examines health challenges facing the San Joaquin Valley and beyond and provides students with an opportunity to engage in, and report on, public health research. Students will develop a capstone project while learning from and connecting to UC Merced and local public health department researchers. Familiarizes students with data and resources utilized by public health researchers to identify and benchmark public health goals.

PH 190.d: Provides intensive treatment of a special topic or problem in public health. Reviews public health theory and research on the issue as well as coverage of the methodological principles and tools used to guide research in the area.

PH 191.t: Special Topics in Public Health II

PH 196.d: Helps students apply classroom lessons as interns at community health organizations. In the classroom, students will read and discuss theories and empirical research, as well as discuss experiences in the field. Concurrently, students will be placed as interns at various public health and community health organizations throughout the San Joaquin Valley and Sierra Foothills.

PH 202.d: Introduces, compares, and applies conceptual frameworks, measures, study designs, and analysis approaches used in the field of epidemiology including causality, measures of disease, measures of association, study design (trials, cohort, case-control, cross-sectional and ecological), biases, screening, statistical inference, and analyzing epidemiologic data.

PH 205.d: Advanced training in Health Services Research including the theoretic foundations, tools, and techniques used by researchers to examine quality of care, access to services, cost/expenditure on health services, translation/dissemination of research, and the state of the health services rural, underserved areas.

PH 206.d: Overview of theory and research on public communication related to health behavior and policy change, including a critical understanding of the effects of mass media in promoting and impeding the achievement of public health goals.

PH 208B.d: Acquaints early-stage graduate students in the core professional knowledge and skills central to Public Health as a discipline and practice, as well as primary avenues for becoming a part of the larger research community. Follows a workshop format in which we will review recent journal articles, become proficient in structuring scientific arguments, and draft, discuss and revise book and article reviews. Lastly, the important issue of ethical research conduct will be addressed.

PH 209A.t: Grant Writing for Public Health I

PH 209B.t: Grant Writing for Public Health II
PH 209B.d: Students will prepare an NIH F-31 application in a weekly structured workshop setting. Students will work closely with their advisors to prepare their research question and specific aims for the April NIH cycle. Students will also learn about other graduate student funding mechanisms, and will become familiar with NIH grantspersonship.

PH 211.t: Introduction to Statistical Methods in Public Health

PH 212.t: Advanced Statistical Methods in Public Health
PH 212.d: Advanced statistics course designed with one overarching goal: to give students the tools necessary to understand, evaluate, and conduct quantitative public health research. The class will concentrate on various quantitative statistical methods for a range of data and research questions relevant in public health research. Students will explore the methods and gain practical skills and experience through class lecture, mini-report, peer-review, literature review, and hands-on data analysis.

PH 222.t: Social Epidemiology: Social Determinants and Population Health Methods

QSB 209.d: Covers broad topics in molecular cell biology hosted by the Molecular and Cell Biology department. Features guest speakers and topics related to molecular biology, cell biology, developmental biology, biochemistry, microbiology, immunology, physiology, neurobiology, and biology education.

QSB 211.t: Advanced Neurobiology: Neurodevelopment and Cell Signaling

QSB 217.t: Lab on a Chip: Developing 3rd World Diagnostics for Global Health

QSB 225.d: Students will learn the basics of DNA copy, transfer, and editing, more advanced topics on recombination and mutagenesis. Course objectives include identification of how DNA and RNA influence inheritance as well as their role in the transfer of genetic information to the cellular level; recognition of how recombination influences mutational changes in bacteria; and the ability to understand the underlying mechanisms of microbial gene expression on a global scale (multiple signaling pathways, regulatory mechanisms from environmental influences).

QSB 227.d: Overview of viruses, focusing on structure, infecting cycle, interactions with host, transmission and methods of detection and control.

QSB 234.t: Frontiers of Molecular and Cellular Biotechnology
QSB 234.d: Current state-of-the-art techniques and concepts in molecular and cellular biotechnology will be introduced. Topics include bioinformatics, molecular dynamics simulations, systems modeling, protein engineering, biomolecular assemblies, drug and gene delivery, recombinant DNA, tissue engineering, single molecule measurements, optogenetics, CRISPR, in vivo imaging, biomaterials, bioelectronics.

QSB 248.t: Advanced Topics in Ecology and Evolution

QSB 249.t: Topics in the History, Philosophy, and Practice of Science

QSB 271.t: Advanced Neurobiology: Brain Dysfunction and Neurodegenerative Diseases

QSB 279.t: Principles of Data Visualization in R for Biologists

QSB 286.d: Provides a graduate level Course-based Research Experience where incoming graduate students will be exposed to cutting-edge concepts in symbiosis, applied math, computational biology, and conservation ecology. Provides students the opportunity to engage in team-based, multidisciplinary research exploring the relationship between various symbiotic models (involving the microbial communities in Leafhoppers, Bobtail squids, and Aiptasia, among others) and climate change.

QSB 289.t: Research Forums in Quantitative and Systems Biology

QSB 290.t: Current Topics in Quantitative and Systems Biology

QSB 291.t: Research Forums in Quantitative and Systems Biology
QSB 291.d: Seminar series covering current topics in quantitative and system biology presented by visiting speakers chosen by QSB faculty and students with occasional presentations by UC Merced faculty and student members of QSB.

QSB 292.t: Quantitative and Systems Biology Group Meeting
QSB 292.d: Meetings to describe current progress and research plans lead by individual QSBGG faculty.

QSB 293.t: Quantitative and Systems Biology Journal Club
QSB 293.d: Student-led presentation, analysis, and discussion of reading assignments from the scientific literature.

ROTC 001B.d: Introduces students to the United States Air and Space Forces and provides an overview of the basic characteristics, missions, and organization of the Air and Space Forces. For AFROTC students only.

ROTC 002B.d: Provides a fundamental understanding of both leadership and team building. The lessons and course flow are designed to prepare students for field training and leadership positions in the detachment. For AFROTC students only.

ROTC 003.d: Introduces the practice of Air Force customs and courtesies, issuing military commands, instructing, directing and evaluating the preceding skills, studying the environment of an Air Force officer, and learning about areas of opportunity available to commissioned officers. For AFROTC students only. Open to students who are members of the Air Force Reserve Officer Training Corps or are eligible to pursue a commission. Course must be taken each semester of the General Military Course.

ROTC 050.t: Introduction to the U.S. Army and Critical Thinking

ROTC 051.t: Introduction to the Profession of Arms

ROTC 104B.d: Utilizes student’s field training experience to take a more in-depth look at leadership. Special emphasis is placed on enhancing communication skills, and why that is important as a leader. Students have an opportunity to try out these leadership and management techniques in a supervised environment as juniors and seniors. For AFROTC students only.

ROTC 105B.d: Prepares college seniors with the foundation to understand their role as military officers and how they are directly tied to our National Security Strategy. Provides an overview of the complex social and political issues facing the military profession and requires a measure of sophistication commensurate with the senior college level. For AFROTC students only.

ROTC 113.d: Engages cadets in advanced leadership experiences that involve planning and controlling military activities of the cadet corps, preparing and presenting briefings and other oral and written communications, and providing of interviews, guidance, and information to increase the understanding, motivation, and performance of other cadets. For AFROTC students only. Course must be taken each semester of the Professional Officer Course.

ROTC 150.t: Training Management and the Warfighting Functions

ROTC 151.t: Applied Leadership in Small Unit Operations

SOC 001.d: The study of groups, culture, collective behavior, classes and caste, community and ecology, role, status, and personality.

SOC 009.d: Examination of political and social mobilization at the local level, including strategies for organization and advocacy.

SOC 010.d: An introduction to the logic and use of statistical techniques in sociological research. By the end of the course, students will have the tools to appreciate and evaluate social research, and a foundation for conducting statistical social research themselves.

SOC 015.d: Provides students with a basic understanding of how to conduct social science research. Topics will include the logic of research design, issues of conceptualization and measurement, the range of data collection methods available to social scientists, and what social scientists do with data once they have collected it.

SOC 020.d: Examines the perceptions, theories, arguments, and proposed solutions to the most vexing social issues. Explanations of these problems can be grouped into micro, meso, and macro levels of analysis. In addition, for the last 100 years researchers have examined the overlap between different social problems.

SOC 070.d: Examines the process of criminal justice in the US and address major theories of crime and deviance. In addition: how individuals and social groups are processed through the criminal court system; historical changes in correctional philosophy and organizational structure; inmate socialization, and social environment changes in U.S. prisons.

SOC 100.d: Sociological theory explores many big questions that people have pondered for centuries, including inequality and why it is tolerated, social change and how it occurs, and social order and how it is maintained. This course provides an introduction to sociological theory, examining both classic and contemporary schools of sociological thought.

SOC 110.t: Social Movements, Protest and Collective Action
SOC 110.d: Introduces the social scientific study of social protest (meaning all forms of non-routine, or contentious politics) and collective action. Examines organized collective efforts to promote or resist change in society that rely, in some part, on non-institutionalized forms of political action.

SOC 132.d: Focuses on how social forces (such as politics, economics, demographics and institutional context) create variation in school practices, and how variation in school practices affects individual student achievement and behavior. Students will also become familiar with presenting, interpreting, and discussing public education data.

SOC 133.d: Focuses on higher education (that is, degree-granting postsecondary education) in the United States, both external forces and contexts (e.g., history, political and social movements, demographic changes, federal and state policy priorities and changes) and institutional settings (e.g., people, cultures, structures, policies). Organized according to three broad questions: (1) How did higher education develop in the United States and why?, (2) How do institutions of higher education work – or do they?, and (3) How does college affect undergraduate students?

SOC 137.d: Explores the experiences of Latinx students in U.S. higher education, focusing on issues of transitions, belonging, identity, engagement (social, cultural, political) and after college trajectories. Through sociological readings, discussions, and student-centered research, examines how race, class, immigration status, and campus policies and cultures shape experiences. Highlights both challenges and strategies Latinx students use to navigate college, fostering a deeper understanding of equity, institutional dynamics, and student agency within contemporary educational contexts.

SOC 145.d: Introduction to some key sociological theories and empirical research on health and illness. Course topics will include the relationship between social structures and the production and distribution of disease; how health and illness are defined and socially constructed; and the link between disease and inequality.

SOC 147.t: The Political Economy of Big Tech

SOC 149.t: Sociology of Science, Medicine, and Technology

SOC 175.t: Topics in Advanced Sociological Research Methods

SOC 180.t: Advanced Issues in Race and Ethnicity

SOC 191.d: Serves as a culminating experience for graduating seniors who are majoring in sociology. Build on the skills students have developed in their prior classes by applying sociological knowledge to a specific, contemporary research topic. Assignments are designed to help students develop additional skills, knowledge, and competencies to engage in contemporary issues using a critical framework.

SOC 201.d: The course's main goal is to help students understand the professional worlds of sociology. The course content will have three primary components: an introduction to academic sociology, an introduction to non-academic sociology, and advice on the successful completion of graduate school in sociology.

SOC 210.t: Graduate Statistics I: Linear Regression Analysis

SOC 215.d: Designed to provide an overview of the major research methodologies and techniques used in the social sciences. By the end of the course, students will have the knowledge and skills they need to design research projects and critically read about and evaluate the research of others.

SOC 284.d: Provides concepts and ideas with which to analyze the diverse contemporary and historical experiences of Latinxs. Interrogates the social forces (such as politics, culture, economics, demographics and institutional context) that create variation in the Latinx experience in the U.S. The purpose is to help us think critically about the role Latinxs play in U.S. society and their diverse experiences.

SPAN 001.d: Introduction to speaking, reading, writing, and understanding Spanish. Classes will be conducted in Spanish.

SPAN 002.d: Introduction to speaking, reading, writing, and understanding Spanish. Classes will be conducted in Spanish.

SPAN 003.d: Review of Spanish grammar with emphasis on building speaking and writing skills and on readings to build cultural understanding. Classes conducted in Spanish.

SPAN 010.d: For native speakers with limited experience in grammar and composition. Emphasis on formal language study and writing. Course conducted in Spanish. Native speaker proficiency required.

SPAN 011.d: For native speakers with limited experience in grammar and composition. Emphasis on formal language study and writing. Course conducted in Spanish.

SPAN 014.t: Introduction to Nahuatl Literature, Language and Culture

SPAN 060.t: Introduction to Chicano/a Culture and Experiences

SPAN 103.d: To develop a student's abilities to communicate in spoken and written Spanish, we emphasize the importance of the interaction between writer, reader, purpose and message. We focus on the four major modes of writing: description, narration, exposition and argumentation. Oral practice is also be a major component in this course.

SPAN 105.t: Claiming Identity in the Hispanic World

SPAN 106.t: Freedom and Revolution in the Hispanic World

SPAN 108.d: Provides advanced-intermediate and advanced level students of Spanish with the Spanish business vocabulary and expressions used to carry out business with Hispanic individuals or companies. The course will focus on the development of communicative skills and communicative strategies for business.

SPAN 111.t: Empire, The Postcolonial, and Representation: Reading East & West

SPAN 114.t: Latinx in Children's Literature and Film
SPAN 114.d: Engages students in an in-depth study of Latino/a/xs in children's literature and film, with special attention to issues of representation and self-representation, reception, publishing, markets, stereotypes, historical evolution, bilingualism, and other linguistic and cultural issues. Combines film analysis and literary criticism to explore how Latino/a/xs have been represented and have represented themselves in these media. In addition, the course exposes students to social and cultural aspects of the Latino/a/x experience in the U.S. that are essential to this type of analysis (including demographics, gender, class, and race nuances) as well as to pedagogical and educational considerations. Taught in Spanish.

SPAN 121.t: Spanish Early Modern and Modern Emotions

SPAN 123.t: Race and Gender in Contemporary Spanish Literature

SPAN 140.t: Indigenous and Latin American Colonial Literature and Culture

SPAN 143.t: Nation and Identity in Contemporary Latin American Literature

SPAN 144.t: Race and Gender in Caribbean Cultural Production

SPAN 145.t: Latin American Dictatorship Literature and Film

SPAN 146.t: Environmental Violence in Latin American Film and Literature

SPAN 147.t: The Boom and Post-Boom as World Literature

SPAN 149.t: The Fantastic, Magical Realism, Realism, and Testimonials

SPAN 151.t: Diasporas and Exiles in Latin America

SPAN 153.t: Bilingualism and Borders in Hispanic Literatures

SPAN 160.d: Focuses on Spanish-English, English-Spanish translation, including translating text from different sources, learning about the translation process, and reviewing Spanish advanced grammar while acquiring new vocabulary.

SPAN 180.t: Topics in Hispanic Languages and Cultures
SPAN 180.d: In-depth study of Spanish Languages and/or Hispanic Culture. Possible topics include Latin American and Spanish Film, the Mexican Corrido, Gender and Latin American Popular Music.

SPAN 190.d: Explores in-depth a literary, linguistic, or cultural topic. Readings and activities emphasize the process of writing a research paper. Students will choose a personal research topic and will present information orally and by writing a final research paper.

SPRK 010.d: Introduces students to life at a research university. Students focus on the nature of inquiry by exploring a particular topic over the course of the semester. Students learn how to generate and answer research questions by applying appropriate methods. For more information on specific SPRK sections, visit https://ge.ucmerced.edu/spark. Restricted to first-year students only.

SPRK 010H.d: Introduces students to life at a research university. Students focus on the nature of inquiry by exploring a particular topic over the course of the semester. Students learn how to generate and answer research questions by applying appropriate methods. For more information on specific SPRK sections, visit https://ge.ucmerced.edu/spark. Restricted to first-year students only.

USTU 015.t: Living Learning Community: Pathways to Student Success

USTU 016.t: Living Learning Community: Pathways to Student Success

USTU 030.d: Assists undergraduates with navigating the research environment while obtaining research and creative skills, defining academic interests and objectives, and in becoming part of the university research community. Students will reflect on their research experience, receive supplemental support from staff to navigate the research process, and explore and prepare for graduate school and careers.

USTU 040.d: Taken in parallel with an external undergraduate internship or other experiential learning activity with instructor approval, students will complete at least 120 hours of internship/career-related experiences over a minimum of five weeks during the semester/summer enrollment period. Students must have been offered and accepted an internship or other career related position to enroll in the course. UC Merced follows the National Association of Colleges and Employers (NACE) Criteria for Internships. Students will need to fill out a pre-course survey and submit their offer letter.

USTU 101.t: College Student Development: Encouraging Community, Sense of Belonging, and University Engagement

HON 002H.d: Emphasizes creativity, innovation, and the development of new knowledge through an interdisciplinary approach. The focus areas of this sophomore-level course are: Creativity in Personal Development: Understanding how creativity aids in personal growth and well-being; Creativity Across Disciplines: Exploring the application of creativity in various fields, including sciences, arts, and humanities; Creative Solutions to Social Issues: Engaging with social problems and developing innovative solutions. Students will engage in this topic both as creators and spectators, potentially engaging campus and community events and activities. Restricted to University Honors Program students.

HON 003H.d: Focuses on best practices in the development of community engagement projects and research through hands on research and written materials. Students will have opportunities to interact with community members through hands on pedagogies that require students to go out into their community to explore and analyze community needs, as well as through guest speakers and workshops. Students will work together in teams to to develop community projects. Restricted to University Honors Program students.

WRI 001.d: Development of critical reading, thinking, and academic writing ability. Intensive practice in analysis of college-level texts and in expository writing and revision. Section placement based on the student's UC Entry Level Writing Requirement Exam score. Completion with a grade of C or better meets University of California Entry Level Writing Requirement. Intended for students who have not placed into WRI 010 or completed ELWR. Students who have placed into WRI 010 may not take this course.

WRI 010.d: Development of college-level skills in effective use of language, analysis and argumentation, organization and strategies for creation, revision and editing.

WRI 010H.d: Development of college-level skills in effective use of language, analysis and argumentation, organization and strategies for creation, revision and editing.

WRI 090.t: Intersections of Creative and Professional Writing
WRI 090.d: Examines the relationship between artistic and utilitarian writing techniques and priorities. Students will generate texts in various genres of creative writing and professional writing), with primary focus on why texts are constructed in different ways for multiple purposes and varied audiences.

WRI 101A.t: Special Topics in Writing for the Psychological Sciences

WRI 103.t: Research Design and Methods in Writing Studies

WRI 107.t: Writing with AI: Ethics, Practice, and Futures

WRI 116A.t: Special Topics in Writing for the Natural Sciences

WRI 117.t: Writing for the Social Sciences and Humanities
WRI 117.d: Studies and practices reading and writing in social science research, emphasizing the interpretation, articulation, and presentation of quantitative and qualitative data. Focuses on disciplinary conventions and style, through projects such as research proposals, literature reviews, case studies, field notes, object and artifact analyses, interviews, ethnographies, and academic posters.

WRI 119A.t: Special Topics in Writing for Engineering

WRI 122.d: Engages the study and practice of expressive modes of persuasion. Students will pursue advanced work in special topic areas, within rhetorical theory and practice.

WRI 125A.t: Intermediate Topics in Creative Writing: Poetry

WRI 125B.t: Intermediate Topics in Creative Writing: Fiction

WRI 125C.t: Intermediate Topics in Creative Writing: Creative Nonfiction
WRI 125C.d: Following the introductory creative writing coursework, students in this course deepen their understanding and process of writing and analyzing creative nonfiction. Students connect to genres and hybrid forms of creative nonfiction and place their process and production of creative nonfiction into contemporary context.

WRI 125D.t: Intermediate Topics in Creative Writing: Drama

WRI 130.d: Analysis and practice of writing, researching, and delivering professional oral presentations including speech scripts, visual aides (print, electronic, and multimedia), and various related documents. Typical formats include prepared and impromptu presentations for specific audiences and purposes.

WRI 131A.d: Theoretical and practical approaches to journal editing in academic, creative, and professional genres. Engaging a range of stylistic, content, layout, and ethical concerns for digital and print journals, students address the demands of reviewing and editing various stages of manuscript preparation, from content to copyediting.

WRI 131B.d: Practical approaches to editing the Vernal Pool, UC Merced’s undergraduate literary journal. Students coordinate the journal’s editorial flow and manage stages of submission. Students engage author inquiries and editorial board suggestions for sustainably producing the journal, engaging a range of content, layout, and ethical concerns for publication.

WRI 150.d: In this advanced workshop students will produce creative and critical work in one of the following genres: fiction, playwriting, poetry, or creative nonfiction.

WRI 180B.d: Provides a structured, mentored capstone experience to reflect on and articulate learning in Writing Studies and to prepare materials for post-graduate audiences. Part two of a two-course sequence.

COGS 103.t: Introduction to Neural Networks in Cognitive Science

ECON 163.t: Economics of Investments, Futures, and Options

ENVE 162.t: Modeling and Design of Energy Systems

GASP 001.t: Introduction to Media and Performance Studies
